newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament may vote on partial budget.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament may vote on partial budget.

text.p: A senior Russian communist, sounding a conciliatory note before a parliamentary debate on the 1997 budget, said on Tuesday that parliament might approve a partial budget to allow the government to carry on working.

Interfax news agency quoted parliament chairman Gennady Seleznyov, speaking after a meeting with President Boris Yeltsin, as saying the lower house might approve a budget for three months "so the government's hands are not tied".
The State Duma has already rejected the government's draft budget once and is due to discuss the spending plans again this week, probably on Friday.
Deputies say the draft does not adequately meet the needs of those who lost out under Russia's painful market reforms.

But government officials, determined to keep a tight rein on spending to win funds from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), have accused deputies of dragging their feet on approving legislation which underpins the budget.
They say Russia urgently needs a new tax code, but accuse the Duma of delaying this.
"Unfortunately, tax reform is being postponed," Deputy Finance Minister Sergei Shatalov told a news conference.
"A lot of positive and very necessary decisions are not ready yet. We shall go into 1998 with a new tax policy, but we are entering 1997 with the old tax system."
The Duma is due to discuss a package of tax amendments on Wednesday. Shatalov said the proposals would raise 30-35 trillion roubles ($5.43 billion to $5.43 billion) in 1997.
The IMF has twice delayed paying Russia tranches of a three-year $10 billion loan because it is worried about low tax revenues.
IMF officials say they are looking for evidence of a sustainable improvement in tax collection before approving the payments of the loan.
The fund's chief representative Thomas Wolf said on Tuesday that the IMF could decide next week whether to recommend releasing the cash.

But the next regular monitoring mission from the IMF would probably not arrive in Moscow until the week after that. "The assessment is under way now and will probably be completed by early next week," he said.
"If it is positive then there would likely be a board meeting around mid-month and right after that the regular monitoring mission would arrive."
The IMF board takes a final decision on whether to pay tranches of loans given to member countries.
Russian officials, mindful of IMF demands, have stressed that revenue collection has improved and they have set up a special emergency committee to force tax debtors to pay.
A handful of companies, including carmaker Avtovaz, face the threat of bankruptcy and plan to hold managers personally responsible if companies do not pay their taxes on time.

Interfax news agency quoted Finance Minister Alexander Livshits as saying the current three-year loan would be Russia's last credit from the IMF because Russia would be cooperating with the international community in a different way by the time the loan expired.
Russia tapped international financial markets last month, raising $1 billion in its first sovereign eurobond since the 1917 Bolshevik revolution brought the communists to power. ($1=5522 Rouble)
